<reason>Both debaters delivered a high-level policy exchange, but Side B won by systematically dismantling the economic feasibility of Side A's alternative while cleanly resolving the pressure on its own case. Side A scored an early point by exposing the timing gap between demolition displacement and future property tax revenues, but Side B persuasively answered that pre-demolition stipends can be fronted from existing funds and replenished by subsequent tax surges. More decisively, Side B's pressure questions forced Side A to concede that heavy replacement mandates would stop owners of existing rentals from selling, shrinking redevelopment to vacant or commercial lots while relying on rent control for existing units. Side B capitalized on this concession in the final rounds, showing that freezing the residential footprint manufactures the very vacancy scarcity that locks out working-class families and undermines relocation vouchers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B3.2], [B4.3], and [B5.1]-[B5.3], Side B dismantled Side A's claim that land prices would simply adjust downward to absorb heavy replacement mandates, forcing Side A to admit in [A4.2] that existing rental owners would not sell and then showing how that freeze creates chronic corridor-wide scarcity.</best_rebuttal>
